heading: C++ awaits a real Yon endpoint
summary: A C++ service gets its HTTPClient with `[[Needs]] GreetingClient& greetingClient;` and waits for it with `co_await`. A method that returns `Task<void>` or `Task<T>` is a C++20 coroutine; the page awaits it like any asynchronous service method. The client class in `client/remotes` declares `Task<Greeting> read();` under `[[GetRequest("/greeting")]]`, and Tachyon writes the method. The request goes to the server of the page: the same origin, without cookies, through the browser transport that Rust and C# use. The answer becomes the typed `Greeting` model from `client/models`, read by the codec that Tachyon generates for it. A failed request throws `tachyon::http::HttpRequestException`, whose `code()` is the code of the browser transport, such as `HTTP_STATUS`; when the exception leaves the method, the page's promise rejects with that code. `{id}` in a request path takes the parameter of the same name, `[[RequestBody]]` sends a parameter as the JSON body, `[[RequestParam]]` adds it to the query and `[[RequestHeader("X-Name")]]` sends it as a header. The client types follow .NET's System.Net.Http: `tachyon::http::HttpClient`, `HttpRequestMessage`, `HttpResponseMessage` and `HttpContent` (ADR 0099). Cached, ClearCache and Setup adapters are not in C++ yet; the build refuses Cached in C++ Tac code with TY1308. The server half of this example is a plain JavaScript controller. A controller in TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Go, Dart, Ruby, Lua or C++ answers in the same way (see Controllers), so this section shows only the browser side in other languages.
